summary:
Consensual same-sex conduct has been decriminalised in Fiji since the Crimes Act 2010 came into force on 1 February 2010, repealing the colonial-era Penal Code offence (Article 175) that carried a maximum of fourteen years' imprisonment. Enforcement of that offence was documented into 2005: in April of that year two men, one of them an Australian tourist, received two-year prison sentences, and the presiding judge described the acts as "so disgusting... any decent person vomit". Human Rights Watch urged that the charges be dropped and the men released, citing Fiji's 1997 constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination.

Arrests ended before the statute changed. In July 2006 the Fijian High Commissioner confirmed an official policy that men engaging in consensual gay sex would no longer be arrested, four years before decriminalisation took legal effect. The practical end of enforcement did not follow from a court ruling but from executive policy.

Fiji was among the first countries in the world to write sexual-orientation non-discrimination into its constitution, in 1997, alongside South Africa. The 2013 Constitution reinstated that protection and expanded it to gender identity and gender expression, a formulation described in regional policy analysis as unique worldwide. Sexual-orientation discrimination in employment has been prohibited since 2007, and health professionals are barred from attempting to change a person's sexual orientation.

The constitutional guarantee has produced no implementing mechanism for trans people. Legislative and policy frameworks permit no change of gender marker on official documents and do not recognise traditional third-gender identities, and the resulting marginalisation and discrimination are documented in the 2023 Asia Pacific Alliance case study on legal gender recognition in Fiji. A visitor whose passport marker does not match their presentation has no domestic route to alignment.

No same-sex marriage or civil union is available: the Marriage Act 2002 defines marriage as between one man and one woman. Intersex bodily autonomy is unprotected by law.

The political and religious climate behind the enforcement era remains part of the record. Days after the April 2005 sentences, Prime Minister Laisenia Qarase rejected international pressure to legalise gay sex, calling homosexuality a sin in what he described as a conservative Christian nation. Public health bodies linked the criminalisation regime to the undergrounding of sex work and the spread of HIV.
tangentialFactors:
Fiji's constitutional position is unusual in both directions: it was the second country in the world, after South Africa, to enshrine sexual-orientation non-discrimination, and its 2013 text carries gender identity and expression protection described as unique worldwide, yet neither protection has been converted into statutory procedure. The gap between headline constitutional text and lived implementation is the central turbulence in the record.

The traditional third-gender role of vaka sa lewa lewa is recognised in Fijian culture and has historical standing in the community, but it carries no legal status. Cultural recognition and legal recognition are separate questions here, and only the former exists.

Contemporary sources disagree about the basic criminal-law position. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, states in its body text that same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 2010, while its at-a-glance panel still flags same-sex relations as illegal. The GlobalGayz country page, which is undated and predates the 2013 Constitution, states that sexual-orientation and gender-identity discrimination was not banned; that claim has been overtaken by the 2013 Constitution.

Enforcement history is short and recent enough to matter to expectations: convictions were handed down in April 2005, a no-arrest policy was confirmed in July 2006, and the statutory repeal came only in February 2010. Prime Minister Qarase's 2005 statements show the domestic political reception of external pressure during that window.
localsOnly:
Residents have had statutory protection against sexual-orientation discrimination in the workplace since 2007, and health professionals are prohibited from attempting to change a person's sexual orientation. These are resident-facing entitlements with no evidence in the inventory of a complaints mechanism or enforcement record.

Legal gender recognition does not exist. No legislative or policy framework permits a change of gender marker, and traditional third-gender identities are not recognised in any official process, despite the 2013 Constitution's protection on gender identity and expression. The Asia Pacific Alliance case study records the resulting marginalisation and discrimination as a documented outcome rather than a projection.

LGBTI organisations cannot register, according to Outright International's country overview. The inventory does not indicate the legal basis or the date of that restriction.

Intersex people have no statutory bodily-autonomy protection, and the cultural standing of vaka sa lewa lewa does not translate into any legal status for people who occupy that role.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: Outright International's overview carries an internal contradiction. Its body text records decriminalisation in 2010 while its at-a-glance panel flags same-sex relations as illegal. The inventory does not resolve which reflects the current position of that source's data, and the Crimes Act 2010 date is corroborated independently by Human Rights Watch, PinkNews and GlobalGayz.

Unresolved: the claim that LGBTI organisations cannot register appears only as an at-a-glance flag in one source, with no legal basis, ministry, or date given. Whether this restriction is current, and whether it applies to all civil-society registration or to a specific category, is not sourced.

Unresolved: no source in the inventory reports an enforcement mechanism, penalty, or decided case under the 2013 Constitution's gender-identity and gender-expression protection, or under the 2007 workplace protection. The absence of documented litigation is not evidence that none exists.

Unresolved: the GlobalGayz page is undated and pre-2013, and the Sydney Morning Herald and PinkNews items date from 2005 and 2006. Their value is as evidence of the enforcement era; none of them speaks to present-day conditions.

Not sourced: entry, visa and border-screening practice for travellers whose passport gender marker does not match their presentation, and any airport or immigration screening that could disclose a traveller's trans status. The inventory addresses domestic law only.
